In geometry, a '''line''' is a set of [[point]]s in a particular [[metric space]] isometric to the [[real line]].

== Formal definition ==

Let $\mathcal{X}=(S,d)$ be a [[metric space]].

$L \subseteq S$ is a '''line''' in $\mathcal{X}$ if

$$
\exists f:\mathbb{R} \to L,\\
\begin{cases}
f(\mathbb{R})=L \\
d(f(a),f(b))= |a-b|,\,  \forall a,b \in \mathbb{R}
\end{cases}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q2296}}</ref>

{{Hidden example}}
In the '''Manhattan metric plane''' $\mathbb{M}^2=(\mathbb{R}^2,d_1(A, B) = |x_A - x_B| + |y_A - y_B|)$<ref>{{#cite:Q2293}}</ref>:

Every line is the image of a parametrisation with general form

$$
\vec{L}(t)=\bigl(\alpha x(t),\ \beta(t+C-x(t))\bigr),
\qquad t\in\mathbb R,
$$

where $\alpha,\beta\in\{-1,+1\}$,$C\in\mathbb R$, and $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, non-decreasing, and $1$-Lipschitz, i.e., $0\le x(t)-x(s)\le t-s\qquad(s<t)$

[[File:Manhattan-plane-lines.png|center|500px|Examples of lines in the Manhattan plane $\mathbb{M}^2]]

{{Hidden proof}}
By definition,
$$
L:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad \vec{L}(t)=(x(t),y(t)),
|x(t)-x(s)|+|y(t)-y(s)|=|t-s|
\qquad \forall s,t\in\mathbb R. \tag{1}
$$

Assume $s<t$, then

$$
|x(t)-x(s)|+|y(t)-y(s)|=t-s. \tag{2}
$$

Let $u \in \mathbb{R}$, then $L(s),L(u),L(t) \in \mathbb{M}^2$ are three colinear points, so $\forall u: s<u<t$, by colinearity,

$$
|x(t)-x(s)|+|y(t)-y(s)| = |x(t)-x(u)|+|y(t)-y(u)| + |x(u)-x(s)|+|y(u)-y(s)|
$$

Since $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$, by triangular inequality of real numbers ($|a-c| \le |a-b|+|b-c|$)

$$
\begin{cases}
|x(t)-x(s)| \le |x(t)-x(u)| + |x(u)-x(s)| \\
|y(t)-y(s)| \le |y(t)-y(u)| + |y(u)-y(s)|
\end{cases}\\ \\
\therefore 
\begin{cases}
|x(t)-x(s)|=|x(t)-x(u)|+|x(u)-x(s)|, \\
|y(t)-y(s)|=|y(t)-y(u)|+|y(u)-y(s)|;
\end{cases}
$$

Hence $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$, $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are monotone functions

$\therefore \exists, \alpha,\eta\in\{-1,+1\}$ such that $\alpha x(t),\eta y(t) $ are both non-decreasing functions of $t$.

$$
\therefore \text{(2)} \Rightarrow \alpha(x(t)-x(s))+\eta(y(t)-y(s))=t-s, \tag{3}
$$

Separate $t$-terms and $s$-terms via algebraic manipulation

$$
\alpha x(t)+\eta y(t)-t
=
\alpha x(s)+\eta y(s)-s,\, \forall s,t \in \mathbb{R}
$$

Hence

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb{R}: \alpha x(t)+\eta y(t)-t=C,\, C \in \mathbb{R} \\
\Rightarrow \alpha x(t)+\eta y(t)=t+C,\, C \in \mathbb{R}
\Rightarrow y(t) = \beta(t+C-x(t)),\, C \in \mathbb{R}, \beta = \eta^{-1} \in \{-1,1\}
$$

Hence

$$
\vec{L}(t)=\bigl(\alpha x(t),\ \beta(t+C-x(t))\bigr),
\qquad t\in\mathbb R,
$$

where $\alpha,\beta\in\{-1,+1\}$,$C\in\mathbb R$, and $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, non-decreasing, and $1$-Lipschitz, i.e., $0\le x(t)-x(s)\le t-s\qquad(s<t)$

{{End hidden}}
{{End hidden}}

== Properties ==

=== Colinearity ===

If $L$ is a line in a given metric space, for any three points $A,B,C \in L$, if $AC \ge AB \land AC \ge BC$, then $AC=AB+BC$.<ref>{{#cite:Q2296}}</ref>

== Notation ==

A line that passes through two points $A,B$ are often denoted $(A,B)$<ref>{{#cite:Q2300}}</ref> or $L_{AB}$.
